title: How to Keep an AliDropship Store Stable Through Updates
excerpt: Self-hosted stores rarely break from traffic. They break from untested updates. Set up staging, a tested backup, and a short smoke checklist before the next release.
body: A self hosted dropshipping store gives you control over hosting, themes, and data, and along with it comes every maintenance task that control implies. Most outages in this setup do not come from traffic spikes. They come from an update applied straight to production: a plugin release that conflicts with the theme, a server side version change, or a pricing rule that silently stops syncing. Treating the store as software rather than as a finished asset is the habit that keeps revenue predictable through the year.

Put staging in place before you need it. A staging copy running the same plugins, the same theme, and a recent data snapshot lets you test an update against real content instead of guessing. If your host does not offer one click staging, a subdomain with a copied file tree and database takes an afternoon to build and pays for itself the first time it catches a fatal error before your customers do. The operating rule is simple: no plugin, theme, or version change touches the live store until someone has clicked through it on staging.

Run two routines on the live environment. Before every change, take a full backup of files and database and confirm you can actually restore it, because a backup nobody has tested is only a guess. After every change, work through a short smoke checklist: place a test order through checkout, trigger one supplier sync, confirm pricing updates landed, and load the cart and a category page as a logged out visitor. Most breakage shows up within two minutes of that checklist and stays invisible without it.

Sequence updates by risk rather than by notification order. Security patches go out the same day. Feature releases wait for a quiet window and for release notes that tell you what actually changed. Major version jumps earn their own maintenance slot and a rollback plan you have already written down. Bundling three unrelated updates into one push makes it impossible to identify which one caused a problem, which is exactly how a fifteen minute task becomes a lost weekend of support tickets.

Keep a change log even when the team is one person. Record the date, what changed, and the result of your smoke test. When the store behaves oddly three weeks later, that log shortens diagnosis from hours to minutes, and it doubles as documentation the day you hand development or fulfillment work to someone else. Pair it with an uptime ping or a synthetic checkout check so you hear about downtime from your own tooling instead of from a customer asking where their order is.

Finally, decide what you will automate and what stays manual. Automatic minor updates save time on low risk plugins, but anything touching checkout, payments, or your import pipeline deserves a human click through on staging first. Review that split once a quarter as your plugin list changes. The DTCwise Dropshipping category at /category/dropshipping keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing, and the AliDropship listing at /tool/alidropship is the place to confirm what the plugin expects from your hosting stack before you schedule the next round of updates.
